params.style: faceless, fast cuts, bold captions, calm narration
params.niche: Psychology & human behavior (biases, habits, social dynamics)
params.niche_summary: Short, curiosity-driven explanations ("why your brain does X") work well in Shorts. Generic people and city stock footage plus calm narration carries them fully. Arabic in particular has few serious psychology channels: the largest Arabic psychology/body-language channel still hasn't reached 1M subscribers.
example_topics: Why we remember embarrassing moments for years (the spotlight effect)
3 signs someone is manipulating you, according to psychology
Why crowds make smart people act dumb
What your phone habits say about your dopamine
params.cta: Follow for a daily brain bias check

options.label: 1. Why You Get Great Ideas in the Shower
options.detail:
Explains the 'shower effect' where mind-wandering during routine, non-demanding tasks releases dopamine and shifts the brain into the default mode network, unlocking creative epiphanies. Shows fast-paced b-roll of flowing water, city walks, and sudden realizations.
Hook (en): Stop trying so hard to think.
Hook (fr): Arrête de forcer tes réflexions.
Why: Creativity and overthinking hacks regularly go viral on Shorts because everyone experiences sudden shower insights; recent 2022-2023 cognitive psychology experiments by Zac Irving confirmed the exact mechanics behind mind-wandering and task incubation.

options.label: 2. Why Big Plates Trick Your Appetite
options.detail:
Reveals the Delboeuf Illusion, showing how the exact same portion size looks drastically smaller on a larger plate, unconsciously forcing your brain to serve more food and feel hungrier. Visualized with geometric circle contrasts and aerial shots of plated meals.
Hook (en): Your plate is controlling your appetite.
Hook (fr): Ton assiette contrôle ton appétit.
Why: Everyday health and perceptual illusions have exceptionally high shareability and comment rates due to people testing the visual illusion directly on screen in the first 5 seconds.

options.label: 3. Why Strangers Like You More Than You Think
options.detail:
Breaks down the 'Liking Gap'—a systematic cognitive bias where people consistently underestimate how much a conversation partner enjoyed talking to them and how positive their first impression was. Uses urban candid pedestrian interactions and coffee shop footage.
Hook (en): They liked you more than you think.
Hook (fr): Ils t'ont apprécié bien plus que prévu.
Why: Social anxiety and self-doubt content are evergreen drivers of high engagement and saves on Shorts; this provides instant emotional relief backed by solid empirical data from Boothby et al.
